column4: The section's opening-word root f-j-r is developed as water breaking out before darkness; this ayah uses al-fajr (ٱلْفَجْرِ) for dawn recitation, preserving the root's opening-of-darkness sense beside the water image.

The section defines the wadi as a flood channel; Abraham describes settling his descendants in an uncultivated valley (بِوَادٍ غَيْرِ ذِى زَرْعٍ) and asks God for fruit, a specific dry-valley counterpart to the flood-bearing valley and its measured yield.

The section recalls Thamud cutting rock homes in the valley; in the Hijr episode, people carve houses from mountains and feel secure (يَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ ٱلْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا ءَامِنِينَ), making the rock-built safety vulnerable to the punishment that follows.

The section says Thamud carved rock in a valley; Salih addresses the same people as mountain-house cutters (تَنْحِتُونَ مِنَ ٱلْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا), giving the repeated carving scene its own warning context.

God tells Moses that Pharaoh has transgressed (إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ); the section's named ṭ-gh-y root links that moral excess to water leaving its measure and also names Pharaoh among the overreaching rulers.
Moses is again sent to Pharaoh, who has transgressed (إِنَّهُۥ طَغَىٰ); this repeated formulation makes the section's water-overflow sense of ṭ-gh-y audible in the ruler's excess.

This begins the water scene completed in 25:49: winds come as heralds of mercy and God sends pure water from the sky (مَاءً طَهُورًا), supplying the rain whose revival and drink the next ayah describes.

After 25:49's reviving rain, this ayah says God distributes the water among people so they may remember, while many refuse; it adds the human response to the provision the section says people misread.

The section's spring, rain and sweet-water notes meet the question about the water people drink (ٱلْمَآءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ); 56:69–70 continue by asking who sends it and whether it could be made bitter.

The section traces provision to water poured from above; this ayah asks whether people bring their drinking water down from the rain cloud (ءَأَنتُمْ أَنزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ ٱلْمُزْنِ) or God does, locating its source with the speaker.

The section names عَذْب as pleasant fresh water beside عَذَاب; this ayah says God could make drinking water bitter-salty (أُجَاجًا) and asks why people are not grateful, making drinkable rain a bounded provision.

The section follows water emerging through earth and treats measured water as provision; this ayah asks who could bring flowing water if it sank into the ground (مَآءُكُمْ غَوْرًا), exposing how easily that provision could be hidden.

The section names divine honoring and provision before the surah corrects the wealthy person's claim; this ayah identifies pushing away the orphan (يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ) as the contrary human measure of honor.

The section's abundance-and-restriction test turns on what people do with provision; this ayah rebukes failing to urge food for the needy (طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ), giving the social consequence of misreading wealth as honor.

The section contrasts the cloud expected to bring rain with a painful punishment and describes punishment poured from above; this ayah says Lot's people were rained upon (وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهِم مَّطَرًا), a rain-word used for destruction rather than drink or growth.

The section's rain scene can turn from expected gift to punishment; this ayah describes the rain on Lot's people and calls it an evil rain (فَسَآءَ مَطَرُ ٱلْمُنذَرِينَ), a direct contrary use of the same weather image.

The section says punishment is poured down from above and recalls Ad's expected rain; in Lot's destruction this ayah specifies that stones of baked clay are rained upon the overturned towns (وَأَمْطَرْنَا عَلَيْهَا حِجَارَةً), making precipitation itself the punishment.
